title: 🛡️ Practice ⭐⭐: what was done, and who is named

questions.prompt: Rewrite this sentence so that it begins with the fountain instead of the council: "The town council repaired the old fountain of Nabeul last winter."

options.text: The old fountain of Nabeul were repaired by the town council last winter.
The old fountain of Nabeul was repair by the town council last winter.
The old fountain of Nabeul repaired by the town council last winter.
The old fountain of Nabeul was repaired by the town council last winter.

questions.explanation: "The old fountain of Nabeul was repaired by the town council last winter." is right: the object of the active sentence moves to the front, the verb becomes be plus the past participle, and be takes the tense of the active verb, which was a past simple, so it becomes was. "The old fountain of Nabeul were repaired by the town council last winter." gives be a plural form, but the new subject, one fountain, is singular. "The old fountain of Nabeul was repair by the town council last winter." leaves the participle unfinished: after be the verb must be repaired, never repair. And "The old fountain of Nabeul repaired by the town council last winter." has no be at all, and without be there is no passive; read as it stands, it says the fountain did the repairing.

questions.prompt: Nizar is planning the next month of his human rights club. Complete his note: "We only have ___ left before the exams, but that is enough to finish the poster."

options.text: a little weeks
a few weeks
much weeks
a lot of weeks

questions.explanation: "a few weeks" is right: weeks can be counted one by one, so they take a few, and a few carries exactly the meaning the note needs, not many but enough, which is why Nizar can still add but that is enough. "a little weeks" uses the quantifier kept for nouns you cannot count, such as time, money or work; you may say a little time, never a little weeks. "much weeks" makes the same mistake and adds a second one, since much belongs to questions and negatives rather than to a plain affirmative sentence. And "a lot of weeks" is well built but says more than enough, which fights with the word only and with the whole sense of the note.

questions.prompt: A student magazine is being edited before it goes to the printer. In which of these sentences does the by phrase give the reader nothing, so that the editor should cut it?

options.text: Our poster was torn down by somebody during the night.
The new rules were written by two pupils of the third year.
The prize was awarded by the mayor of El Kef.
The photographs were taken by Emna's grandmother.

questions.explanation: "Our poster was torn down by somebody during the night." is the one to cut: by somebody names nobody. It tells the reader only that a person did it, which every action already implies, so the sentence loses nothing and gains three words by becoming Our poster was torn down during the night. In "The new rules were written by two pupils of the third year." the agent is the surprise of the sentence, since rules are usually written by adults. In "The prize was awarded by the mayor of El Kef." the agent says how official the ceremony was. And in "The photographs were taken by Emna's grandmother." the agent is a person the reader could never have guessed. Keep the agent when it is news, drop it when it is unknown, obvious or everybody.

questions.prompt: Emna is completing the Verb and Noun table of the lesson. She has already written the noun "oppression" in the right-hand column. Which verb goes in the left-hand column, opposite it?

options.text: to oppose
to press
to impress
to oppress

questions.explanation: "to oppress" is the verb: take the ending -ion off oppression and the verb is there, exactly as declaration gives to declare, promotion gives to promote and commitment gives to commit. "to oppose" is close in sound and in letters but heads another family, the one that gives opposition and an opponent: to oppose is to be against something, while to oppress is to treat a group cruelly because you hold power over it. "to press" is simply the short verb hidden inside the long one, and it means to push on something; sharing letters is not sharing a family. And "to impress" means to make somebody admire you, and it gives the noun impression, not oppression.

questions.prompt: This sentence has to go on a notice at an information desk, and a notice never spends words on who does the work: "People speak three languages at this information desk." Which version belongs on the notice?

options.text: Three languages are spoken by people at this information desk.
Three languages is spoken at this information desk.
Three languages are spoken at this information desk.
Three languages are speaking at this information desk.

questions.explanation: "Three languages are spoken at this information desk." is the notice: the object of the active sentence, three languages, becomes the subject, be stays in the present because the active verb speak was in the present, and the agent disappears because people means everybody and therefore means nothing. "Three languages are spoken by people at this information desk." is correct English but keeps that empty agent, which is precisely what a notice cuts. "Three languages is spoken at this information desk." gives be a singular form although the subject, three languages, is plural. And "Three languages are speaking at this information desk." replaces the participle with the -ing form, which turns the languages into speakers.

questions.prompt: Mouna's grandmother tells a school magazine: "I left school at eleven, because the nearest one was four kilometres away and there was no bus. I learnt to read at forty-two, in an evening class that a neighbour opened in her own front room. My own daughters walked to school every morning, and neither of them ever missed a year." What does this testimony let you conclude?

options.text: She was not allowed to go to school at all.
Distance, not a refusal, ended her schooling.
Her daughters left school at the same age as she did.
The evening class was organised by the town hall.

questions.explanation: "Distance, not a refusal, ended her schooling." is what the testimony gives you: she names one cause and only one, four kilometres and no bus. "She was not allowed to go to school at all." is contradicted by her very first words, since leaving school at eleven means she had been going to it for years. "Her daughters left school at the same age as she did." is the reverse of her last line, where neither daughter ever missed a year. And "The evening class was organised by the town hall." replaces the agent she names with one she never mentions: the class was opened by a neighbour, in her own front room, and a reader may not invent an agent the text does not give.
